hook: She escaped slavery, then went back again and again to lead others to freedom.

pages.x: Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross, around 1822, on a plantation in Maryland. As a small child she was hired out to other families and whipped. Three of her sisters were sold away, and she never saw them again.

As a teenager she was hit on the head by a heavy iron weight that an overseer threw at another enslaved man. For the rest of her life she had seizures, headaches and vivid dreams, which she believed were messages from God.

In 1849, afraid she would be sold, she escaped alone, walking about 145 km by night to Pennsylvania, guided by the North Star. "I had crossed the line. I was free; but there was no one to welcome me to the land of freedom."
She went back to Maryland about 13 times and led around 70 people to freedom, her own family among them, along the Underground Railroad, a secret network of safe houses. People called her Moses.
She travelled in winter, when nights were long, and sang songs as secret signals. She carried a pistol, and later said: "I never ran my train off the track, and I never lost a passenger."
In the Civil War she worked for the Union army as a nurse, scout and spy. In 1863 she guided gunboats up the Combahee River in South Carolina, in a raid that freed more than 700 enslaved people.
After the war she lived in Auburn, New York. Poor herself, she cared for the old and the sick, and fought for women's right to vote. She died in 1913, aged about 91.

pages.x: Tubman freed herself, then risked her life again and again to free others. She is one of the great heroes of American history.
